div.head: “Voracity”: Introduction to Reading Notebook 07.02.02, 1930-1943
div.p: Jeff Westover

Arthur James Balfour claimed that “an impotent voracity for desultory information” is a “most desirable, and a not too common, form of mental appetite” (Notebook 07.02.02, p. 67r). Marianne Moore recorded this statement in the 460-page reading notebook she maintained from 1930 to 1943. Based on the varied content of the notebook and the wide range of subjects in her poetry, it is not hard to see why she took the trouble to record this idea. It provides as good an epigraph for the notebook as any. After all, she had claimed in the 1924 version of “Poetry” that even “business documents” are “important” (New Collected 27). The notebook entry actually involves two sources, for Moore is quoting someone (Balfour) who is quoting someone else (Frederic Harrison) in order to rebut and correct him. The quotation also brings to mind the playful title of a short poem Moore first published in 1947, “Voracities and Verities Sometimes are Interacting” (Spearhead, New Directions, 1947: New Collected 182).

Voracity certainly is the word. The notebook features entries on subjects ranging from contemporary film to meticulous descriptions of exotic and ordinary animals, from information about female tennis players and authors to excerpts on ethics and politics, from inventories of period furniture and varieties of wood to catalogues of music, from book reviews and advertisements to notes on mottoes and heraldry, and from ancient Egyptian artefacts to the history and techniques of typesetting. As in her poems, the notes shift abruptly from one richly detailed topic to another without warning or transition, leaving one to wonder about the motives and circumstances behind the notes and the manner and order in which they were collected over time. In short, the notebook is encyclopedic in scope and chronological in its arrangement, following what she picks up to read at any given moment.

Many of the subjects are familiar enough to fans of Moore’s writing, but some may seem more obscure though not surprising, given her reputation for wide-ranging and detailed knowledge, often on recondite subjects. The notebook gives a sense of how this knowledge was obtained and perhaps retained, though not how it was consulted when she drafted her poems.

While miscellaneous in its overall compass, the notebook provides material relevant to the composition of the following poems, all of which were published in the 1930s except the last four: “The Student” (Poetry, 1932), "No Swan So Fine" (Poetry, 1932), “The Jerboa” (Hound & Horn, 1932), “Camellia Sabina” (Active Anthology, 1933), “The Plumet Basilisk” (Active Anthology, 1933), “The Frigate Pelican” (The Criterion 1934), “The Buffalo” (Poetry, 1934), “Nine Nectarines and Other Porcelain” (Poetry, 1934), “Walking-Sticks and Paperweights and Watermarks” (Poetry, 1936), “Half Deity” (Direction, 1935), “Smooth Gnarled Crape Myrtle” (New English Weekly, 1935), “Virginia Britannia” (Life and Letters Today, 1935), “The Paper Nautilus” (as “A Glass-Ribbed Nest” in the Kenyon Review, 1940), “In Distrust of Merits” (Nation, 1943), “Logic and ‘The Magic Flute’” (Shenandoa, 1956), “O To Be a Dragon” (Sequoia, 1957), and “Leonardo da Vinci’s” (New Yorker, 1959). It also features notes relevant to essays published from the 1930s through the 1950s, including “Charlotte Brontë” (1932), “Feeling and Precision” (1944), “Humility, Concentration, and Gusto” (1949), and “Idiosyncrasy and Technique” (1958).

A few issues that stand out in this notebook include (1) the tensions between the drive to know and the limitations of human knowledge; (2) the visual and material aspects of some forms of language; and (3) aesthetics and culture. In terms of my first issue, the drive to know and the contingencies that thwart it, Moore’s quotation of Albert Einstein in “The Student” that “Science is never finished” sums up well her own quest for knowledge (New Collected 95). Unsurprisingly, the idea of science, or knowledge, being unfinished is demonstrated in the notes on animal behavior and anatomy. Readers will recognize this interest in her animal poems and her frequent epistolary references to animal films, zoos, circuses, and museums of natural history. The animals she studies include various kinds of insects, birds, amphibians, mammals, and fish. Her interest extends to flora as well as fauna, including notes for “Camellia Sabina” and “Nine Nectarines and Other Porcelain.” Moore also records amusing scenes from fiction and biography, striking details about the social life of Victorian England, and catchy phrases from conversations.

Different passages in the notebook attest to Moore’s focus on the limitations on human knowledge, limitations based on the complexity and scale of the cosmos, theological ideas about human nature, and the contingency of categories. For example, in an article about Roger and Francis Bacon in Scientific Monthly by Sanford Fernando, a physicist who taught at Stanford, Moore singles out the following passage about the medieval scholar Roger Bacon’s view of “the fallibility of human reason”:

lg.l: it is certain that never, before God is seen face to face, shall a man know
anything with final certainty. It is impossible therefore for a man to attain
perfect knowledge in this life, & it is exceedingly difficult for him to
attain perfect truth, & he is very prone & disposed toward whatever is
false & empty; wherefore man ought not to boast of his knowledge. (220v-220r)

div.p: This excerpt squares with a traditional Christian emphasis on humility as a virtue. But it appears in a popular article by a professional scientist who singles out Bacon for his emphasis on the importance of evidence-based reasoning. At the same time that Moore demonstrates her appetite for learning about a variety of topics, she testifies to her belief about the inadequacies of human understanding in such passages. This conflicting attitude toward knowing things seems in keeping with Moore’s poetic values of intensive detail, spry syntax, and restraint. In the poems of the thirties, as in the earlier poems “The Octopus” and “Marriage,” she sometimes offers a bewildering array of images and ideas. This can arouse a kind of exhilaration in the reader, but it also points to the challenges of sorting out significance. Perhaps it also cautions readers to acknowledge the complexity, diversity, and contradictory aspects of experience in order to avoid oversimplifying them.

In another notebook entry, Moore records the following excerpt from Rule of the Road, a 1937 book by Anne Byrd Payson: “It may be that certainty is too static for human development & that minds devel. best in uncertainty, that trying to find truth is better than than leaning hard on demonstrable fact.” (230r)

Payson’s statement resembles John Keats’s definition of negative capability as living with uncertainty “without any irritable reaching after facts and reason.” It also parallels the theme of victory over adversity at the heart of some of the Latin mottoes Moore records in this notebook, including one used in a printer’s mark: “Veritas virescit vulnere” (“when wounded, truth just gets fresher”).

Moore wrote an extensive series of notes about typography and printing—an interest especially relevant to “Walking-Sticks, Paperweights, and Watermarks.” The passages about typeface reflect Moore’s personal aesthetics and presumably her earlier editorial work at The Dial. Similar notes about heraldry also attest to a concern with language and visual rhetoric, with visual details and their beauty, and with processes of signification. The notes often reflect Moore’s sense in “The Steeple-Jack” that “it is a privilege to see so / much profusion” (New Collected 93). They also reflect the sharp shifts in reference evident in “The Jerboa,” “The Plumet Basilisk,” and “The Frigate Pelican.” In these and other of Moore’s poems, trains of modifiers build to climaxes that accentuate and energize the nouns they modify. The exuberance that these modifiers convey is matched by the bewilderment and potential confusion associated with complex syntax and shifting metonymic associations.

As I have hinted, the notebook often reflects Moore’s keen interest in flora and fauna. It contains extensive excerpts about jerboas and similar rodents from “Smaller Mammals of North America” by Edward W. Nelson, which appeared in the May 1918 issue of the National Geographic (85r-89v). There is also an array of notes from The Illustrated London News. Similar notes and drawings about amphibians and flora are relevant to “The Plumet Basilisk” (28r-29v; 92v-93r; 108v-110v). Given Moore’s penchant for fusing the human and animal worlds in her poems, many of her notes on culture are also relevant to “The Jerboa” and “The Plumet Basilisk.” For example, notes about cultural artifacts from ancient Egypt are also germane to “The Jerboa” (96r-97v; 98v-99v), and the annotations to the notebook indicate with precision the original sources, some of which Moore shared in her published notes to her poems. The notebook entries reflect Moore’s sustained study of biology and material culture, documenting some of the sources she drew upon to renew and recast the traditions of the bestiary and animal fable in her great animal poems. The notebook is a treasure trove of sources and information Moore drew upon to develop these two major poems, but its miscellaneous nature also omits sources Moore credited, including Raymond L. Ditmars’ Strange Animals I Have Known and George Jennison’s Animals for Show and Pleasure in Ancient Rome.

Many of the entries in this notebook focus on women’s experience and their achievements in the fields of literature, sports, or the arts. There are extensive notes about “Tennis Impressions” by Helen Wills, a major female tennis star of the 1930s (51v-54v). She also takes notes about women writers who lived in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, including notes on a biography of Charlotte Brontë and lively excerpts from Memories of Victorian England by Lucy Bethia Walford (104r-105r) as well as Fanney Burney and Her Friends (124v-125v). In addition, she tracks ads for an edition of Silas Marner by George Eliot and Sarah Josepha Hale’s Woman’s Record, Or Sketches of All Distinguished Women From the Creation to the Present Time (1853).

In the extensive notes she takes about typography, papermaking, and book design, Moore focuses on the materiality of the signifier and its aesthetic effects. She also suggests the connection between the tools required for printed representation and the style of meaning they convey. In particular, one of Moore’s sources addresses the role of margins in printed matter, including William Morris’s view of them and his Kelmscott Press. In “Walking-Sticks,” Moore focuses on the interaction between the physical qualities of paper, words, and even letters, both in the sense of the alphabet and epistolary communication. Like so many of her poems about art, “Walking-Sticks and Paperweights and Watermarks” extols the aesthetic pleasures aroused by objects. The poem does so in order to assess their meaning and value.

Similarly, Moore’s cluster of notes on “The Principles of Film Form,” an article by Sergei Eisenstein, focus on the need to refresh and clarify the perceptions of film-viewers. (Moore also took notes about other articles featured in Close-Up, including Eisenstein’s “An American Tragedy.”) I associate this process with the poet’s more scattered notes about culture and the aesthetic experience. In one passage from her notes, Eisenstein argues that “Montage is not an idea recounted by pieces following each other, but an idea that arises in the collision [boldface in original] of two pieces independent of one another. The Dynamic Principle.) 2 independent ideographical signs (“Shots”) placed in juxtaposition, explode to a new concept.” (61r)

Through her strategic use of boldface and underlining, Moore calls attention to the conflict and synthesis at work in Eisenstein’s conception of montage. A collision of ideas and images occurs in many of Moore’s more challenging poems. So does the goal of improving or heightening the perception of her readers, which is similarly in keeping with Eisenstein’s goal in his praise of what he calls the “dynamic principle”: “I regard the appearance of new concepts & percepts arising in the conflict between usual appearance & special representation as xactly a dynamic occurrence The dynamisation of the perception—a dynamization of the “traditional apprehension” into a new apprehension.” (62v)

A passage quoted in a separate part of the notebook seems related to Eisenstein’s claims here about “a new apprehension”: “Culture (acc to Prof Shaw) is not a mere decoration of the mind, but a means of interpreting oneself to oneself. . . . "the awakening of your consciousness to the . . . value of a life habitually taken for granted." It does not consist in the number of things you know.” (55r)

This passage turns from the tallying of facts to an assessment of their use and value, defining culture as a means for growth and understanding. The act of “interpreting oneself to oneself” emphasizes culture as an action, as a mode of self-cultivation. In this respect it parallels the aesthetic ideal of the nurturing maternal embrace in “The Paper Nautilus.” As Heather Cass White has argued, “The Paper Nautilus” displaced “The Pangolin” as a general statement of poetic value when Moore chose to put it at the end of What are Years, moving “The Pangolin” from that position in her previous book (Adversity & Grace xix). Moreover, the central theme of “The Paper Nautilus,” along with the poem’s reference to paper, aligns it with “Walking-Sticks and Paperweights and Watermarks” by focusing on the general significance of making and enjoying art.

This notebook’s pervasive concern with the value of aesthetic experience and the desirability of acquiring it echoes in several poems. In its extraordinary range and diversity of subject matter, the notebook shows Moore’s robust conception of culture and the complex nature of knowledge. It documents the scope of her learning as well as the network of connections between her poetry and other cultural forms, including cinema, the arts and crafts, sports, and music. The notebook is marked by the abundance she praises in “The Jerboa,” and it reflects her deep devotion to popular science. Finally, it suggests that her poetry is of a piece with the living world it depicts with such gusto.
Works Cited
Moore, Marianne. New Collected Poems. edited by Heather Cass White. Farrar, Straus and Giroux, 2017.
Moore, Marianne. Adversity and Grace. edited by Heather Cass White. ELS Editions, 2012.

In scanning this notebook to create digital images of its pages, the Rosenbach was inconsistent in scanning open-face (verso-recto) or single verso or recto pages. Consequently, although all pages of the manuscript are represented here, there are occasional gaps in the numbering sequence, as listed under Notebook Description. There are no missing pages, just missing recto or verso numbers.
